pr_title: [8.0] Critical fix to output cache; remove OutputCacheEntry recycling
pr_body:
# Critical fix to output cache

Output cache shared buffer in the "multiple people requesting same page" path released prematurely, leading to empty responses.

## Description

Part of net8 work in the output-cache middleware was to reduce allocations; one aspect of this was buffer recycling in the `OutputCacheEntry`, however a late discovery is that this recycling can impact separate requests, due to the `Task` reuse between requests when using "locking" mode (see `_requestDispatcher.ScheduleAsync`). This means that some requests (as a race condition) can get empty responses if the `OutputCacheEntry` was already recycled.

There is no risk of buffer bleed between responses (so: no infosec issue), but: empty responses is a critical failure and must be addressed.

Given the late stage of net8, it is proposed to simply drop the buffer recycling aspect; this puts `OutputCacheEntry` back *exactly where it is in net7*, so this choice is not a regression: we just lose something we wanted to add. We can revisit this when we have time to do this safely, in net9 and possibly back-ported to net8 as a service release. A brief investigation using counting was attempted, but this was not immediately successful, and I'd rather have minimum risk.

A new test shows the failure, and now passes.

Fixes #51009 (note that despite the title, this issue is not specific to any particular output-cache provider)

## Customer Impact

Without the fix, empty responses are possible

## Regression?

- [x] Yes
- [ ] No

[If yes, specify the version the behavior has regressed from]

net7.0, net8 preview 6

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

Resolution chosen with minimal risk rather than perfect solution in mind, that sacrifices some potential buffer reuse; we plan to
implement full buffer reuse by restructuring the shared result cache, allowing us to correctly track active usage, but this is
beyond what we will do "now". This work will be in net9 and optionally backported to a net8 servicing release (tbd).

## Verification

- [ ] Manual (required)
- [x] Automated - new test

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

----

## When servicing release/2.1

- [ ] Make necessary changes in eng/PatchConfig.props

issue_context.title: Content-Length mismatch randomly on high throughput when using  Output Caching
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

When using StackExchange Redis Output Caching we randomly get an error:
```
System.InvalidOperationException: Response Content-Length mismatch: too few bytes written (0 of 5468).
```
We analyzed the key value, and we see that the Content-Length is not part of the cache, this means that this 5468 is calculated from the cached entry, but for some reason, the response is not written and this error appears.  

Output caching with Memory works without this issue. 

**UPDATE**

The number of threads does not meter. The difference is the .NET Version (on the local we had Preview 7 and, on the environment, the latest nightly build). It seems the issue is introduced after RC1 version

### Expected Behavior

No System.InvalidOperationException happening.

### Steps To Reproduce

For the test, we created an Apache JMeter test with 10, 25, and 50 threads calling the API each of the tests contained this error.
We could reproduce the issue when using Output caching on the Debug level, only in the environment with the Docker container connecting to the Redis database.

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

8.0.0-rc.2.23466.4

### Anything else?

As additional context, when the API is called within a single thread sequentially there is not this error. When I introduce a second parallel thread the issue occurs.

@mgravell, @BrennanConroy Is there any chance you can take a look at this?

Thanks
Well, dang. This is going to be a pain. Adding to my "things on fire" list for urgent investigation. I only saw this at the end of my day today - will be next working day to investigate.

I was able to repro when going from preview7 of aspnetcore to rtm of aspnetcore. And I can repro without using Redis.

Looking into it a little since my work day is starting 😛
@BrennanConroy Great news that you created repro, not sure why this is not happening to us with Memory variant.. But we use rc2 on env.
@BrennanConroy well that just went from "bad" to "oh god"; I'm not at a PC so I can't jump on, sorry - my Monday isn't looking fun

Ok I think I found the bug, introduced in RC1 with https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/48328

The issue is that the `OutputCacheEntry` returned from
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/36e03b5be98b34804fcf23a2e9c05a5211e1108b/src/Middleware/OutputCaching/src/OutputCacheMiddleware.cs#L345
can be returned to multiple requests
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/36e03b5be98b34804fcf23a2e9c05a5211e1108b/src/Middleware/OutputCaching/src/DispatcherExtensions.cs#L18
Which was done to reduce hitting the cache multiple times when serving the same cached response.
The problem is that we use potentially pooled memory in the `OutputCacheEntry` and want to clean up that pooled memory once we've served the request, so we dispose the `OutputCacheEntry` at
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/36e03b5be98b34804fcf23a2e9c05a5211e1108b/src/Middleware/OutputCaching/src/OutputCacheMiddleware.cs#L118
Which clears the body and headers which can cause any requests that are sharing the `OutputCacheEntry` to have odd behavior, like already setting the Headers but not having a body anymore, or not having headers or body and responding with an empty 200.

A couple possible fixes:
* Ref count in OutputCacheEntry so we don't dispose an in-use one
* Remove `_outputCacheEntryDispatcher.ScheduleAsync(...)` and always hit the cache so we don't share cache entries

@BrennanConroy excellent investigative work; I'm inclined towards the former, to prevent alloc overhead - some kind of `bool TryReuse()` check returns true if and only if it can increment a counter i.e. it isn't already zero. A little awkward to implement though. I can look on Monday if you're not fancying a distraction.

The "oops we need to fix after rc2" isn't going to be a fun email to write, though ...
Hi everyone, On what version we can test this fix? We tried nightly containers but still getting same issue? Thanks

review_comments: Is the `_recycleBuffers` property still in use? Can be removed if not.

yeah, I was planning to - [have an initial test](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/51067/commits/135c4fa9fd9688c57840b78a3fb713ab8e22cf19) (which shows the problem if we comment/uncomment the `throw;`), but it manifests contrary to my expectations (i.e. we see an actual exception rather than a 5xx http); I'm going to check this test against the "before I touched anything" state, to see if this is just an artefact of the test harness

tested at `b362c450058d7fe3279ffdcc1f6e40beaf828967` (which is "before") - behaviour is identical there, i.e. yes, I think that's a feature of the test harness (presumably we're hooking at a level that doesn't include the global fault handler)
This is also memory coming from the ArrayPool that we're no longer returning?

We set `recycleBuffers` to true in one case
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/9922772d07a7f4d21d2becdb00fb5a206b9807cc/src/Middleware/OutputCaching/src/OutputCacheMiddleware.cs#L431
Are we now adding unnecessary strain on the ArrayPool by not returning that memory?
array pool doesn't care about non-returned buffers - they'll just GC

Sure, but if you drain the array pool it becomes expensive to get an array from the pool. We saw this recently with the IdentityModel package where they weren't disposing an object that had rented memory from the array pool and so it was GCed instead of returned, but then the array pool became empty and it was very expensive to rent new arrays from the pool.

@BrennanConroy right; but if we don't want to leak buffers, we need to either a: implement ref-counting, or b: fetch the memory from somewhere else, and drop *that* on the floor; I had a stab at the ref-counting originally, and ironically: it was that damned missing `throw;` that caused that experiment to fail; we can implement it; consider: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/51131/files

but... that's what I was saying is a bit more "fun"; is it worth deferring that to service release 1 ?
am I understanding correctly though that this takes us back to .NET 7? if so, then it's apparently shippable quality. or is this a place where we will be introducing something new.

> am I understanding correctly though that this takes us back to .NET 7? 

The PR as is doesn't take us all the way back to .NET 7. In .NET 7 we just allocated. This PR reverts to an in-between state, we call `ArrayPool.Rent` but don't call `ArrayPool.Return`.

I think we should either
* run a quick perf test to see if it causes issues 
* just remove ArrayPool.Rent and allocate
* Fix this bug and keep RC1 ArrayPool usage (there is a draft PR by Marc for this)
your judgement, but I'd err towards minimum risk given we have no more previews. .NET 7 was successful.
